claim: Primary murine CTLs coordinate their migration in a process reminiscent of the swarming observed in neutrophils.
source: Primary murine CTLs coordinate their migration in a process reminiscent of the swarming observed in neutrophils.
evidence: The manuscript directly states this observation in the abstract, supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: CTLs engaging cognate targets accelerate the recruitment of distant T cells through long-range homotypic signalling, in part mediated via the diffusion of chemokines CCL3 and CCL4.
source: CTLs engaging cognate targets accelerate the recruitment of distant T cells through long-range homotypic signalling, in part mediated via the diffusion of chemokines CCL3 and CCL4.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments including RNA sequencing, mass spectrometry, and functional assays.

claim: Newly arriving CTLs augment the chemotactic signal, further accelerating mass recruitment in a positive feedback loop.
source: Newly arriving CTLs augment the chemotactic signal, further accelerating mass recruitment in a positive feedback loop.
evidence: This mechanism is described in the abstract and demonstrated through experimental observations and computational modeling.

claim: Activated effector human T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells similarly employ intra-population signalling to drive rapid convergence.
source: Activated effector human T cells and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells similarly employ intra-population signalling to drive rapid convergence.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with human T cells and CAR T cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: CTLs recognising a cognate target can induce a localised mass response by amplifying the direct recruitment of additional T cells independently of other leukocytes.
source: Thus, CTLs recognising a cognate target can induce a localised mass response by amplifying the direct recruitment of additional T cells independently of other leukocytes.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing CTL recruitment without other cell types.

claim: CTLs are key effectors of adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies.
source: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) constitutively migrate as single cells in search of infected or malignant cells (Weninger et al., 2014). CTLs are key effectors of adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies (Guedan et al., 2019), but their efficacy remains limited with solid tumours (van der Woude et al., 2017), which they infiltrate in insufficient numbers (Galon et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Guedan et al., 2019.

claim: The efficacy of CTLs in adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies remains limited with solid tumours.
source: CTLs are key effectors of adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies (Guedan et al., 2019), but their efficacy remains limited with solid tumours (van der Woude et al., 2017), which they infiltrate in insufficient numbers (Galon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to van der Woude et al., 2017 and Galon et al., 2006.

claim: CTLs infiltrate solid tumours in insufficient numbers.
source: CTLs are key effectors of adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies (Guedan et al., 2019), but their efficacy remains limited with solid tumours (van der Woude et al., 2017), which they infiltrate in insufficient numbers (Galon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galon et al., 2006.

claim: CTLs have been thought to arrive at target sites either via random search or following signals by other cell types.
source: Thus far, CTLs have been thought to arrive at target sites either via random search (Krummel et al., 2016) or following signals by other cell types (Feig et al., 2013; Harlin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krummel et al., 2016, Feig et al., 2013, and Harlin et al., 2009.

claim: CTLs employ highly evolved cell-intrinsic search strategies that are more efficient than Brownian motion.
source: They have revealed, for instance, that CTLs employ highly evolved cell-intrinsic search strategies that are more efficient than Brownian motion (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harris et al., 2012.

claim: During priming in lymph nodes, CD8+ T cells can follow local chemoattractant gradients to migrate directionally towards sites of antigen presentation.
source: During priming in lymph nodes, CD8+ T cells can follow local chemoattractant gradients to migrate directionally towards sites of antigen presentation (Castellino et al., 2006; Hickman et al., 2011; Hugues et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castellino et al., 2006, Hickman et al., 2011, and Hugues et al., 2007.

claim: Natural killer (NK) lymphocytes produce chemokines that attract dendritic cells.
source: Recent studies indicate that lymphocytes can recruit each other indirectly into tumours; natural killer (NK) lymphocytes produce chemokines that attract dendritic cells (Böttcher et al., 2018), which in turn can recruit CTLs (Spranger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Böttcher et al., 2018.

claim: Dendritic cells can recruit CTLs into tumours.
source: Recent studies indicate that lymphocytes can recruit each other indirectly into tumours; natural killer (NK) lymphocytes produce chemokines that attract dendritic cells (Böttcher et al., 2018), which in turn can recruit CTLs (Spranger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spranger et al., 2017.

claim: Intravital microscopy is typically restricted to relatively short imaging periods and sub-millimetre fields of view.
source: Although intravital microscopy enables imaging of cellular interactions in the TME in situ, it is typically restricted to relatively short imaging periods and sub-millimetre fields of view (Gabriel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gabriel et al., 2018.

claim: CTLs engaging a cognate tumouroid were rapidly recruited to its edge, where they accumulated over time.
source: CTLs engaging a cognate tumouroid were rapidly recruited to its edge, where they accumulated over time (Figure 1B and Video 1).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B and Video 1.

claim: The marked accumulation of CTLs at the edge of the tumouroid is reminiscent of swarming observed in neutrophils.
source: The marked accumulation of CTLs at the edge of the tumouroid is reminiscent of swarming, the coordinated collective convergence of large numbers of self-propelled individuals, which has been observed in as varied biological systems (Okubo, 1986) as mammals, birds, fish, insects, and, at the cellular level, neutrophils (Lämmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This comparison is made explicitly and supported by citations to Okubo, 1986 and Lämmermann et al., 2013.

claim: CTL accumulation behavior was not observed with control tumouroids lacking cognate antigen.
source: This behaviour was not observed with control tumouroids lacking cognate antigen (Figure 1B and Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B and Video 2.

claim: When an additional CTL population was embedded in the cognate tumouroid where it actively eliminated tumour target cells, the surrounding CTLs amassed at the tumouroid and infiltrated it to a greater extent.
source: When an additional CTL population was embedded in the cognate tumouroid where it actively eliminated tumour target cells (Video 3), the surrounding CTLs amassed at the tumouroid (Figure 1B) and infiltrated it to a greater extent (Figure 1D,E and Video 2).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures and videos.

claim: Enhanced infiltration was also observed into masses constituted of cognate antigen-coated beads.
source: This enhanced infiltration was also observed into masses constituted of cognate antigen-coated beads, which, in contrast to tumour cells, do not progressively give way to additional physical space due to lysis by CTLs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: The introduction of a desensitisation threshold in chemokine concentration, above which agents revert to unbiased motion, was necessary to recapitulate experimental observations in simulations.
source: The introduction of a desensitisation threshold in chemokine concentration, above which agents revert to unbiased motion, was necessary to recapitulate our experimental observations (Figure 1F–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by figures and video showing simulation results.

claim: Surrounding CTLs migrate rapidly and highly directionally towards the edge of a cognate tumour mass.
source: Using this approach, we found that surrounding CTLs migrate rapidly and highly directionally towards the edge of a cognate tumour mass (Figure 2B), containing pre-embedded CTLs at 1:1 or 1:5 ratios with tumour cells, or in the complete absence of pre-embedded CTLs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: CTLs adjacent to control tumouroids exhibited no chemotaxis, albeit some chemokinesis (enhanced speed).
source: By contrast, CTLs adjacent to control tumouroids exhibited no chemotaxis, albeit, interestingly, some chemokinesis (enhanced speed) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Cell-free supernatant from the co-incubation of CTLs with cognate tumour cells attracts other CTLs in a transmigration assay.
source: Indeed, cell-free supernatant from the co-incubation of CTLs with cognate tumour cells (cognate supernatant) attracts other CTLs in a transmigration assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and thus contains the soluble chemoattractants mediating the recruitment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B, and C.

claim: 10-fold dilutions of cognate supernatants also induced CTL transmigration.
source: Interestingly, 10-fold dilutions of cognate supernatants also induced CTL transmigration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the CTL response to the soluble chemotactic factors is highly sensitive.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Recruitment of CTLs was preserved when tumour cells were replaced with polystyrene beads coated with cognate antigen.
source: To distinguish whether the factors originate from CTLs or lysed tumour cells, we replaced tumour cells with polystyrene beads coated with cognate antigen (Figure 2C) and found that recruitment of CTLs was preserved (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C and D.

claim: CTLs engaging cognate targets produce factors that induce distal recruitment via homotypic signalling.
source: CTLs engaging cognate targets therefore produce factors that induce distal recruitment via homotypic signalling.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the bead experiment results.

claim: Tumouroids containing monospecific CTLs and their cognate tumour targets are equally proficient at recruiting T cells of the same, different, and polyclonal specificity.
source: Tumouroids containing monospecific CTLs and their cognate tumour targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) are equally proficient at recruiting T cells of the same (Figure 2E), different (Figure 2F) and polyclonal (Figure 2G) specificity.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures.

claim: No recruitment is observed towards tumouroids containing CTLs engaging non-cognate target cells.
source: No recruitment is observed towards tumouroids containing CTLs engaging non-cognate target cells.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: Production of the homotypic signal requires recognition of specific cognate antigen, but the signal recruits CTLs irrespective of the T cell receptor (TCR) they express.
source: Therefore, whilst production of the homotypic signal requires recognition of specific cognate antigen, the signal recruits CTLs irrespective of the T cell receptor (TCR) they express.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the recruitment experiments with different T cell specificities.

claim: At the onset of the experiment (0 hr), CTLs were distributed uniformly adjacent to both cognate and non-cognate tumouroids.
source: At the onset of the experiment (0 hr), CTLs were distributed uniformly adjacent to both cognate and non-cognate tumouroids (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: After 2 hr, the distribution of CTLs was biased towards the cognate tumouroid.
source: After 2 hr, the distribution of CTLs was biased towards the cognate tumouroid (Figure 3A,B), whereas the CTL distribution adjacent to a control tumouroid remained unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by figures.

claim: Even the most distant CTLs show directional movement towards the cognate tumouroid.
source: Cell tracking analysis revealed that even the most distant CTLs show directional movement towards the cognate tumouroid (Figure 3C,D and Video 6) and reveals a moving wave of chemoattraction over time (Figure 3E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by figures and video.

claim: Cells close to the tumouroid start moving towards it at early timepoints but lose some of their directionality over time.
source: Cells close to the tumouroid start moving towards it at early timepoints but lose some of their directionality over time (Figure 3E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Chemotactic responses can be lost under excess local concentrations of ligand.
source: It has previously been shown that chemotactic responses can be lost under excess local concentrations of ligand (Lim et al., 2018), which could account for the behaviour observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lim et al., 2018.

claim: For cells furthest from the tumouroid, directional migration commences at later timepoints.
source: For cells furthest from the tumouroid, directional migration commences at later timepoints (Figure 3E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: A gradient of diffusing factors is established following cognate interactions between CTLs and tumour cells to induce the long-range chemoattraction of other T cells.
source: These results indicate that a gradient of diffusing factors is established following cognate interactions between CTLs and tumour cells to induce the long-range chemoattraction of other T cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the long-range migration experiments.

claim: PTX inhibits the enhanced average speed and directional migration of CTLs towards cognate tumouroids.
source: PTX inhibits the enhanced average speed and directional migration of CTLs towards cognate tumouroids (Figure 4A), indicating that GPCR ligands mediate the chemoattractive signal.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: GPCR ligands mediate the chemoattractive signal.
source: PTX inhibits the enhanced average speed and directional migration of CTLs towards cognate tumouroids (Figure 4A), indicating that GPCR ligands mediate the chemoattractive signal.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the PTX inhibition experiment.

claim: The formation of small CTL clusters around malaria-infected hepatocytes required GPCR signalling.
source: This result is consistent with previous work where the formation of small CTL clusters around malaria-infected hepatocytes required GPCR signalling (Cockburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cockburn et al., 2013.

claim: Neutrophils employ lipid signalling via leukotriene B4 to swarm.
source: Unlike neutrophils that employ lipid signalling via leukotriene B4 to swarm (Lämmermann et al., 2013), this result suggests that chemokines, which are sensed by GPCRs, underpin homotypic signalling in CTLs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lämmermann et al., 2013.

claim: Chemokines underpin homotypic signalling in CTLs.
source: Unlike neutrophils that employ lipid signalling via leukotriene B4 to swarm (Lämmermann et al., 2013), this result suggests that chemokines, which are sensed by GPCRs, underpin homotypic signalling in CTLs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the GPCR inhibition results.

claim: The following GPCR ligands were identified as differentially expressed: CCL1, CCL3, CCL4, CCL9, and XCL1.
source: Differentially expressed genes were filtered for secreted factors, among which the following GPCR ligands were identified: Chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 1 (CCL1), CCL3, CCL4, CCL9, and X-C motif chemokine ligand 1 (XCL1) (Figure 4B); their upregulation was further validated by quantitative reverse transcription PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomics analysis reveals that CCL1, CCL3, CCL4, and XCL1 are more abundant in cognate supernatant.
source: Mass-spectrometry-based proteomics analysis of cognate versus non-cognate secretomes reveals that CCL1, CCL3, CCL4, and XCL1 are more abundant in cognate supernatant (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 2), confirmed by quantitative detection assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C and supplementary files.

claim: The recombinant chemokines CCL3, CCL4, CCL5, and CXCL12 could attract CTLs in transwell migration assays.
source: The recombinant chemokines CCL3, CCL4, CCL5, and CXCL12 could attract CTLs in transwell migration assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), in each case effectively inhibited by the corresponding neutralising antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: Only CCL3 inhibition consistently disrupted CTL transmigration in transwell chambers towards cognate supernatants.
source: However, only CCL3 inhibition consistently disrupted CTL transmigration in transwell chambers towards cognate supernatants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Directional migration towards a cognate tumouroid in 3D matrices was abolished only when both CCL3 and CCL4 were blocked using neutralising antibodies.
source: Directional migration towards a cognate tumouroid in more physiological 3D matrices was abolished only when both CCL3 and CCL4 were blocked using neutralising antibodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), indicating that these two chemokines act redundantly in the homotypic attraction.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: CCL3 and CCL4 constitute the diffusive homotypic signal that attracts distant CTLs during target engagement.
source: Therefore, CCL3 and CCL4 constitute the diffusive homotypic signal that attracts distant CTLs during target engagement.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the neutralization experiments.

claim: Secreted CCL3 forms a gradient from the site of antigen-specific target engagement.
source: Secreted CCL3 forms a gradient from the site of antigen-specific target engagement, visualised by in situ capture and staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: CTLs sustain their ability to secrete CCL3 and CCL4 even after disengagement from cognate targets.
source: Strikingly, CTLs sustain their ability to secrete CCL3 and CCL4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), and to recruit distant T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), even after disengagement from cognate targets.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: Tumour cells that constitutively secrete both CCL3 and CCL4 induced enhanced rapid directional motility in CTLs.
source: To confirm that CCL3 and CCL4 secretion are sufficient to induce chemoattraction in distant CTLs, we engineered tumour cells that constitutively secrete both chemokines (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A,B), or CCL3 or CCL4 alone. Secreting tumouroids induced enhanced rapid directional motility in CTLs (Figure 4D), swarming and infiltration (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C–H).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: CTLs infiltrate CCL3/CCL4-secreting cognate tumouroids as efficiently as tumouroids within which CTLs are actively engaging cognate targets.
source: CTLs infiltrate CCL3/CCL4-secreting cognate tumouroids as efficiently as tumouroids within which CTLs are actively engaging cognate targets (Figure 1D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and references Figure 1D.

claim: In the absence of cognate antigen, CTLs do not stop at the edge of secreting tumouroids and thus infiltrate them deeper.
source: In the absence of cognate antigen, CTLs do not stop at the edge of secreting tumouroids and thus infiltrate them deeper (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E and H).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3E and H.

claim: CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours consistently recruit more endogenous NK cells than contralateral control tumours.
source: We next established an in vivo model to investigate if CCL3/CCL4-secretion influences endogenous leukocyte recruitment to tumours engrafted in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), and showed that CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours consistently recruit more endogenous NK cells than contralateral control tumours (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1, CCR2, or CCR3 did not have any effect on CTL recruitment.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1, CCR2, or CCR3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C) did not have any effect, whereas targeting CCR5 with Maraviroc or the CCR2/CCR5 dual antagonist Cenicriviroc abrogated the homotypic recruitment of CTLs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Targeting CCR5 with Maraviroc or the CCR2/CCR5 dual antagonist Cenicriviroc abrogated the homotypic recruitment of CTLs.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of CCR1, CCR2, or CCR3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C) did not have any effect, whereas targeting CCR5 with Maraviroc or the CCR2/CCR5 dual antagonist Cenicriviroc abrogated the homotypic recruitment of CTLs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Polyclonal T cells isolated from Ccr5 knockout mice were not efficiently recruited towards cognate tumouroids.
source: Furthermore, polyclonal T cells isolated from Ccr5 knockout mice (Ccr5-/-; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) were not efficiently recruited towards cognate tumouroids (Figure 5A) or cognate supernatant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: When wild type (WT) and Ccr5-/- CTLs were co-embedded around a cognate tumouroid, the Ccr5-/- population exhibited severely impaired swarming and infiltration depth.
source: When wild type (WT) and Ccr5-/- CTLs were co-embedded around a cognate tumouroid, the Ccr5-/- population exhibited severely impaired swarming (Figure 5B,C), and infiltration depth (Figure 5D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5B, C, and D.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs exhibited a reduced capacity to eliminate cognate tumour masses.
source: Moreover, Ccr5-/- CTLs exhibited a reduced capacity to eliminate cognate tumour masses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), despite fully functional antigen-specific cytotoxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H) and chemokine secretion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs have fully functional antigen-specific cytotoxicity.
source: Moreover, Ccr5-/- CTLs exhibited a reduced capacity to eliminate cognate tumour masses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), despite fully functional antigen-specific cytotoxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H) and chemokine secretion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs have functional chemokine secretion.
source: Moreover, Ccr5-/- CTLs exhibited a reduced capacity to eliminate cognate tumour masses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G), despite fully functional antigen-specific cytotoxicity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H) and chemokine secretion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: CCR5 mediates the chemokine signal underpinning the homotypic recruitment of T cells.
source: These findings demonstrate that CCR5 mediates the chemokine signal underpinning the homotypic recruitment of T cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the CCR5 knockout and inhibition experiments.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs showed impaired homing into CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours in vivo.
source: In vivo, Ccr5-/- CTLs that were co-transferred with WT CTLs showed impaired homing into CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and, in contrast to WT CTLs, did not bind fluorescent CCL3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs did not bind fluorescent CCL3 in vivo.
source: In vivo, Ccr5-/- CTLs that were co-transferred with WT CTLs showed impaired homing into CCL3/CCL4-secreting tumours (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B) and, in contrast to WT CTLs, did not bind fluorescent CCL3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Impaired CCR5-dependent recruitment through dense tumour tissue was observed in response to the acute injection of a molecular hydrogel enabling shear-reversible containment of recombinant CCL3.
source: We also observed impaired CCR5-dependent recruitment through dense tumour tissue in response to the acute injection of a molecular hydrogel enabling shear-reversible containment of recombinant CCL3 (Nisbet et al., 2018; Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Video 7).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Video 7.

claim: The presence of tumour-reactive CTLs markedly increased the overall recruitment of all non-cognate CTLs into the tumours.
source: The presence of tumour-reactive CTLs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E,F) markedly increased the overall recruitment of all non-cognate CTLs into the tumours (Figure 5F).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: Recruitment of Ccr5-/- OT1 CTLs into tumours containing activated gBT1 CTLs was compromised compared to WT CTLs.
source: Furthermore, recruitment of Ccr5-/- OT1 CTLs into tumours containing activated gBT1 CTLs was compromised compared to WT CTLs.
evidence: This observation is stated in the text.

claim: Ccr5-/- CTLs cleared tumours with comparable efficacy to WT CTLs.
source: However, Ccr5-/- CTLs cleared tumours with comparable efficacy to WT CTLs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Sustained release of CCL3 and CCL4 is sufficient to promote CCR5-dependent homing into tumours in vivo.
source: Together, these results indicate that sustained release of CCL3 and CCL4 is sufficient to promote CCR5-dependent homing into tumours in vivo, and that the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs in a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CCR5+ CTLs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vivo experiments.

claim: The presence of tumour-reactive CTLs in a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CCR5+ CTLs.
source: Together, these results indicate that sustained release of CCL3 and CCL4 is sufficient to promote CCR5-dependent homing into tumours in vivo, and that the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs in a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CCR5+ CTLs.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the in vivo experiments.

claim: Homotypic CTL recruitment via CCR5 is likely not the only or primary signalling circuit that results in CTL tumour infiltration or clearance.
source: Homotypic CTL recruitment via CCR5 is, however, likely not the only or primary signalling circuit that results in CTL tumour infiltration or clearance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental results.

claim: Human effector T cells activated by anti-CD3/CD28 antibody-coated beads upregulate CCL3 and CCL4 expression.
source: Human effector T cells activated by anti-CD3/CD28 antibody-coated beads were found to upregulate CCL3 and CCL4 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) as previously reported (Cristillo et al., 2003) and produced supernatant that attracts additional effector T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citation.

claim: Supernatant from activated human T cells attracts additional effector T cells.
source: Human effector T cells activated by anti-CD3/CD28 antibody-coated beads were found to upregulate CCL3 and CCL4 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) as previously reported (Cristillo et al., 2003) and produced supernatant that attracts additional effector T cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6A.

claim: When co-embedded with activating beads, human T cells recruit distant T cells, which exhibit increased directionality and swarming.
source: When co-embedded with activating beads in place of a tumouroid, human T cells recruit distant T cells, which exhibit increased directionality (Figure 6B,C) and swarming (Figure 6D–F and Video 8).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by multiple figures and video.

claim: Directional recruitment of human T cells is abolished by Cenicriviroc.
source: This directional recruitment is abolished by Cenicriviroc (Figure 6C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Human CD19+ EphA2-specific CAR T cells efficiently killed glioblastoma cells.
source: Human CD19+ EphA2-specific CAR T cells efficiently killed glioblastoma cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: When EphA2-specific CAR T cells were embedded in a tumouroid with glioblastoma cells, surrounding CAR T cells swarmed towards the tumouroid.
source: When EphA2-specific CAR T cells were embedded in a tumouroid with glioblastoma cells, surrounding CAR T cells swarmed towards the tumouroid, whereas no recruitment was observed when CAR T cells were co-embedded with EphA2-negative fibroblasts in the tumouroid (Figure 6G–I and Video 9).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6G–I and Video 9.

claim: No recruitment was observed when CAR T cells were co-embedded with EphA2-negative fibroblasts in the tumouroid.
source: When EphA2-specific CAR T cells were embedded in a tumouroid with glioblastoma cells, surrounding CAR T cells swarmed towards the tumouroid, whereas no recruitment was observed when CAR T cells were co-embedded with EphA2-negative fibroblasts in the tumouroid (Figure 6G–I and Video 9).
evidence: This observation is stated in the text and supported by Figure 6G–I and Video 9.

claim: Upon activation either via the TCR or an engineered CAR, human CTLs engage in homotypic chemokine signalling, thereby amplifying the recruitment of additional T cells to an effector site.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that upon activation either via the TCR or an engineered CAR, human CTLs engage in homotypic chemokine signalling, thereby amplifying the recruitment of additional T cells to an effector site.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the human T cell and CAR T cell experiments.

claim: Swarming has been described for neutrophils during parasite infection in the lymph node and in response to tissue injury.
source: At the immune cell level, swarming has been described for neutrophils, during parasite infection in the lymph node (Chtanova et al., 2008) and in response to tissue injury (Lämmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chtanova et al., 2008 and Lämmermann et al., 2013.

claim: CTLs engaging targets employ homotypic signalling via secretion of the chemokines CCL3 and CCL4 to accelerate the direct recruitment of distant T cells.
source: Here, our data reveal that CTLs engaging targets employ homotypic signalling via secretion of the chemokines CCL3 and CCL4 to accelerate the direct recruitment of distant T cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: As additional antigen-specific CTLs are recruited and engage cognate targets, they contribute to the chemoattractive signal, thus further amplifying CTL recruitment in a positive feedback loop, which leads to swarming behaviour.
source: As additional antigen-specific CTLs are recruited and engage cognate targets, they contribute to the chemoattractive signal, thus further amplifying CTL recruitment in a positive feedback loop, which leads to swarming behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the mechanism.

claim: CTLs closest to the source of the chemotactic signal become desensitised over time and lose directional bias.
source: Interestingly, it appears as though CTLs closest to the source of the chemotactic signal become desensitised over time and lose directional bias, which could be due to exposure to excess ligand concentrations (Lim et al., 2018) or rapid internalisation of the CCR5 receptor (Escola et al., 2010).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by citations.

claim: In lymph nodes, naïve CD8+ T cells follow CCR5 ligands, including CCL3 and CCL4, to migrate towards dendritic cells interacting with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
source: Pioneering work had uncovered that in lymph nodes, naïve CD8+ T cells follow CCR5 ligands, including CCL3 and CCL4, to migrate towards dendritic cells interacting with CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Castellino et al., 2006; Hickman et al., 2011; Hugues et al., 2007), to optimise the efficiency of T cell priming.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castellino et al., 2006, Hickman et al., 2011, and Hugues et al., 2007.

claim: Maximal priming and generation of CTLs in infected or draining lymph nodes during antiviral and antitumour responses depend on CCR5 expression on T cells.
source: Maximal priming and generation of CTLs in infected or draining lymph nodes during antiviral and antitumour responses also depend on CCR5 expression on T cells (González-Martín et al., 2011; Hickman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to González-Martín et al., 2011 and Hickman et al., 2011.

claim: CTLs can independently induce mass recruitment around an antigen-specific target.
source: Our findings reveal that CTLs can independently induce mass recruitment around an antigen-specific target.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Lymphocytes can promote the recruitment of distant lymphocytes into peripheral tissues.
source: Our data also reveal that lymphocytes can promote the recruitment of distant lymphocytes into peripheral tissues, thus far thought to only occur indirectly through the action of professional antigen-presenting cell (APC) intermediaries (Spranger et al., 2017; Böttcher et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by citations.

claim: The concept of bacterial quorum sensing has been applied to coordinated population responses by T cells, where the amplification of local T cell densities was shown to occur via differentiation or proliferation.
source: Although the concept of bacterial quorum sensing has been applied to coordinated population responses by T cells, the amplification of local T cell densities was shown to occur via differentiation or proliferation (Antonioli et al., 2019), relatively long-term effects compared to the rapid directional recruitment of distal CTLs discussed here.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Antonioli et al., 2019.

claim: CTLs engaging tumour targets that do not present cognate antigen induce chemokinesis in distant CTLs.
source: CTLs engaging tumour targets that do not present cognate antigen induce chemokinesis in distant CTLs, which could be mediated via the induced secretion of netrins, autotaxin, or semaphorins (Boneschansker et al., 2016; Katakai et al., 2014; Takegahara et al., 2005).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by citations.

claim: Only CTLs that have directly engaged a cognate antigen-presenting target secrete the homotypic recruitment signal that induces chemotaxis in distant T cells.
source: Importantly, only CTLs that have directly engaged a cognate antigen-presenting target secrete the homotypic recruitment signal that induces chemotaxis in distant T cells.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Unconjugated CTLs exposed to cognate supernatant did not themselves upregulate CCL3 or CCL4 expression.
source: Unconjugated CTLs exposed to cognate supernatant (containing abundant CCL3, CCL4, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interferon gamma and tumour necrosis factor) did not themselves upregulate CCL3 or CCL4 expression (Supplementary file 1 and 2).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by supplementary files.

claim: The individuals of a CTL population exist in three distinct states: a 'searcher' state, a 'responder' state, and an 'engager/recruiter' state.
source: We thus propose that the individuals of a CTL population exist in three distinct states: a 'searcher' state whilst scanning for cognate antigen unaffected by the homotypic signal; a 'responder' state when they sense the homotypic signal and move rapidly towards the effector locus; and an 'engager/recruiter' state upon target cell recognition when they concurrently deliver their effector function and secrete CCL3 and CCL4 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The first CTLs to recognise a cognate target directly transition from search into engagement and recruitment.
source: The first CTLs to recognise a cognate target directly transition from search into engagement and recruitment, whereas subsequent cells arrive in a responder state.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: CTLs can remain in an exclusive recruiter state for nearly 24 hr following target elimination in the absence of active engagement.
source: It is interesting to note that CTLs can also remain in an exclusive recruiter state for nearly 24 hr following target elimination in the absence of active engagement (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: The multistate recruitment model explains prior observations of non-specific T cells only deeply infiltrating tumour tissues in the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs.
source: This multistate recruitment model explains prior observations of non-specific T cells only deeply infiltrating tumour tissues in the presence of tumour-reactive CTLs (Boissonnas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boissonnas et al., 2007.

claim: Although antigen recognition is specific, the chemoattractive signal that is raised to amplify recruitment is generic and thus able to recruit a repertoire of CTLs regardless of their TCR specificity.
source: Although antigen recognition is specific, the chemoattractive signal that is raised to amplify recruitment is generic and thus able to recruit a repertoire of CTLs regardless of their TCR specificity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: There have been prior observations of bystander recruitment of effector T cells to sites of inflammation or tumours initiated by unrelated antigen.
source: Indeed, there have been prior observations of bystander recruitment of effector T cells to sites of inflammation or tumours initiated by unrelated antigen (Boissonnas et al., 2004; Topham et al., 2001; Ariotti et al., 2015; Hickman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Studies that compared tumours infiltrated by leukocytes ('hot') to those that excluded immune cell infiltration ('cold') identified more abundant CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in hot tumours.
source: Interestingly, studies that compared tumours infiltrated by leukocytes ('hot') to those that excluded immune cell infiltration ('cold') identified more abundant CCL3, CCL4, and CCL5 in hot tumours (Chakravarthy et al., 2018; Spranger et al., 2015), including via single-cell transcriptomics that ascribed their expression to CD8+ T cells (Jerby-Arnon et al., 2018; Roider et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging.
source: We demonstrated that CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging, and revealed that the presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the in vivo findings.

claim: The presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.
source: We demonstrated that CTLs exhibit chemotaxis towards CCR5 ligands within dense tumour tissue by intravital imaging, and revealed that the presence of antigen-specific CTLs within a tumour promotes the recruitment of distant CTLs into the tumour in a manner partially dependent on CCR5.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the in vivo findings.

claim: The activation of intratumoural CTLs promotes the recruitment of not only CTLs, but also natural killer cells and myeloid cells.
source: The activation of intratumoural CTLs were found by others to promote the recruitment of not only CTLs, but also natural killer cells and myeloid cells (Rosato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rosato et al., 2019.

claim: Alternate chemokine signalling circuits centred on CXCR3 and BLT1 have been implicated in CTL tumour trafficking and infiltration.
source: Alternate chemokine signalling circuits centred on CXCR3 and BLT1 have been implicated in CTL tumour trafficking and infiltration (Chheda et al., 2016; Chow et al., 2019; Mikucki et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: IFNγ can induce CXCL9 and CXCL10 secretion in various intermediary cells, including tumour-infiltrating myeloid cells.
source: Furthermore, IFNγ, produced by activated CTLs and abundant in inflamed tumours, can induce CXCL9 and CXCL10 secretion in various intermediary cells, including tumour-infiltrating myeloid cells (Dobrzanski et al., 2001; Gordon-Alonso et al., 2017; Hickman et al., 2015), which may enhance the role of CXCR3 in homing.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with severe autoimmune diseases.
source: CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with severe autoimmune diseases (Mackay, 2014), and CCR5 ligands are abundant in the upper respiratory tract during acute hyperinflammation associated with viral infection (Chua et al., 2020); silencing homotypic recruitment may well prove beneficial in such contexts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mackay, 2014 and Chua et al., 2020.

claim: CCR5 ligands are abundant in the upper respiratory tract during acute hyperinflammation associated with viral infection.
source: CCR5-expressing CTLs have been associated with severe autoimmune diseases (Mackay, 2014), and CCR5 ligands are abundant in the upper respiratory tract during acute hyperinflammation associated with viral infection (Chua et al., 2020); silencing homotypic recruitment may well prove beneficial in such contexts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020.

claim: The homotypic recruitment mechanism could be exploited to enhance control over positioning and tissue infiltration of T cells in adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies.
source: Ultimately, the homotypic recruitment mechanism could be exploited to enhance control over positioning and tissue infiltration of T cells in adoptive cell transfer immunotherapies, not least given our findings that engineered CAR T cells, following antigen recognition via the CAR, are able to induce homotypic recruitment of distal T cell populations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.
